findings.title: Token exchange drops the redirect_uri used to obtain the code
findings.body: OAuthLoginView always sends redirect_uri on the GitHub authorize redirect (built at the redirect just above), but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. OAuth 2.0 requires that if redirect_uri was included in the authorization request, the token request must repeat that exact value; GitHub otherwise rejects the code with bad_verification_code or redirect_uri_mismatch. Every install then dies on the generic authenticity error after the user consents. The new tests stub the token endpoint and never assert the POST body, so they cannot catch this.

findings.title: Installer check is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet
findings.body: The new GitHub-user check is the point of this change, but GitHubInstallation only compares pipeline state github_authenticated_user to metadata sender after an Integration row already exists and has no OrganizationIntegration. If Integration.DoesNotExist — the normal case when the browser returns with installation_id before the installation webhook is processed, or if the webhook never arrives — dispatch calls pipeline.next_step() immediately. build_integration never reads github_authenticated_user either, so the OAuth login is discarded. Any Sentry user who completes OAuth as themselves can still bind an arbitrary Sentry GitHub App installation_id (leaked or raced) to their organization and inherit that installation's repo access. The stated mismatch failure does not cover the path that actually creates the integration.

findings.title: Sender lookup assumes metadata shape and 500s otherwise
findings.body: After finding an ACTIVE Integration with no OrganizationIntegration, the code compares the OAuth login to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guard. This pipeline never writes sender (build_integration only copies state["sender"], which nothing in the new flow sets), and older rows may not have that key or may store a non-dict. A missing or malformed sender raises KeyError/TypeError instead of the installation error page, so re-link/reinstall of those installations 500s and the security check never returns a controlled failure. The same block also re-fetches with status=ACTIVE and turns a non-active Integration into the generic authenticity error, which is a behavior change from the previous re-link path.

findings.title: Not-found install test never reaches the GitHub 404 path
findings.body: test_installation_not_found no longer starts a pipeline via init_path. It hits setup_path with only installation_id (no setup_action=install), which PipelineAdvancer treats as no pipeline and redirects to / with "Invalid request.", then issues a second request whose state (ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05) is not the pipeline signature used everywhere else (9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3). That cannot exchange a code, cannot call the stubbed 404 installation endpoint, and cannot produce the old "The GitHub installation could not be found." error. The assertion was weakened to the generic authenticity string, so the 404 contract is untested and this test should fail or pass for the wrong reason.

findings.title: User-mismatch test signs the pre-mutation webhook body
findings.body: test_github_user_mismatch loads INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE, sets sender.login to "attacker", then posts that modified JSON with the original hardcoded X-Hub-Signature sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486. The HMAC is over the raw body, so it cannot match after the mutation. If signature verification is on, the webhook is rejected, no Integration sender is stored, and the later check for "Invalid installation request." is the same string OAuthLoginView returns for a bad state — so the test does not prove the OAuth login was compared to the installing user. There is also no case where sender login matches the stubbed octocat user and an already-existing Integration is allowed to proceed.
